title: Write Borrow Pattern
story: Sometimes you need to rearrange, update, or transform data in place. The write borrow pattern gives you exclusive access to modify — nobody can read or write while you work.
why: The write borrow pattern guarantees exclusive mutation access, eliminating the possibility of data corruption from concurrent modifications.
analogy: A write borrow is like booking a private editing room — you go in alone, make your changes, and when you're done, the room (data) is available for others again.
try_it: Write a fn shuffle(items: &mut Vec[Int]) that rearranges elements randomly. Verify the Vec has the same length after shuffling.
tips: Use &mut when your function needs to modify data — the signature tells callers clearly
&mut auto-coerces to & for reads — you don't need separate read and write references
Chain &mut calls sequentially, not simultaneously — only one &mut can exist at a time
After a &mut function returns, the original variable is usable again
common_mistakes: Using owned parameters when &mut would work — consuming the value is unnecessary
Trying to call two &mut functions on the same data at once — wrap in scopes
Forgetting that &mut is exclusive — even read-only access is blocked during &mut
